title: Comparing
why: Comparing is essential for giving your opinion: with יוֹתֵר, פָּחוֹת, מִ־ and הֲכִי, you can say more, less, than and the most. You'll practice on a great Israeli classic: Tel Aviv versus Jerusalem.

{"lessons": ["

More… than, less… than

To compare, Hebrew puts יוֹתֵר (yoter, more) or פָּחוֹת (pakhot, less) in front of the adjective, and \"than\" is מִ־, attached to the next word, just like in מִפָּרִיז (from Paris). So Hebrew literally says \"hotter from Paris.\" There is no \"-er\" ending: \"hotter\" is simply \"more hot.\"

תֵּל אָבִיב יוֹתֵר חַמָּה מִפָּרִיז.Tel Aviv is hotter than Paris. [tel aviv yoter khama mi-pariz]
הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס פָּחוֹת יָקָר מֵהַמּוֹנִית.The bus is less expensive than the taxi. [ha-otobus pakhot yakar me-ha-monit]

The adjective agrees with the first noun, as usual. Cities are feminine: תֵּל אָבִיב יוֹתֵר חַמָּה.

When?ExamplePronunciation
before most letters: the letter gets a dotמִתֵּל אָבִיבmi-tel aviv
before א ה ח ע רמֵחֵיפָהme-kheifa
before the article הַ־מֵהַבַּיִתme-ha-bayit

Don't mix up \"than\" and \"that\": שֶׁ־ means \"that,\" as in \"I think that…\" In a comparison, \"than\" is always מִ־: יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל מִ־.

", "

The most: הֲכִי

For the superlative, just one word: הֲכִי (hakhi) in front of the adjective. The noun keeps its article, the adjective doesn't:

זֹאת הַמִּסְעָדָה הֲכִי טוֹבָה בָּעִיר.This is the best restaurant in town. [zot ha-mis'ada hakhi tova ba-ir]

No special words like \"better\" or \"best\": you simply say הֲכִי טוֹב (\"the most good,\" best) and יוֹתֵר טוֹב (\"more good,\" better). הֲכִי also works with a verb: מָה אַתָּה הֲכִי אוֹהֵב? (what do you like most?).

Equality: כְּמוֹ (like, as… as). Excess: מִדַּי (too), after the adjective.

חֵיפָה יָפָה כְּמוֹ תֵּל אָבִיב.Haifa is as beautiful as Tel Aviv. [kheifa yafa kmo tel aviv]
הַדִּירָה יְקָרָה מִדַּי.The apartment is too expensive. [ha-dira yekara midai]

In speech, people say יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל; in writing, you'll also see the reverse order, גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר. Both mean \"bigger.\" And \"much more\": הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר (harbe yoter).

", "

Tel Aviv or Jerusalem?

Israelis love comparing their two big cities. Here's what you often hear:

תֵּל אָבִיב יוֹתֵר חֲדָשָׁה וְיוֹתֵר רוֹעֶשֶׁת.Tel Aviv is newer and noisier. [tel aviv yoter khadasha ve-yoter ro'eshet]
יְרוּשָׁלַיִם יוֹתֵר עַתִּיקָה וְיוֹתֵר שְׁקֵטָה.Jerusalem is older and quieter. [yerushalayim yoter atika ve-yoter shketa]
בַּחֹרֶף יְרוּשָׁלַיִם הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר קָרָה מִתֵּל אָבִיב.In winter, Jerusalem is much colder than Tel Aviv. [ba-khoref yerushalayim harbe yoter kara mi-tel aviv]
הַדִּירוֹת בְּתֵל אָבִיב הֲכִי יְקָרוֹת בָּאָרֶץ.Apartments in Tel Aviv are the most expensive in the country. [ha-dirot be-tel aviv hakhi yekarot ba-arets]

בָּאָרֶץ (ba-arets), \"in the country\": that's how Israelis talk about Israel in everyday life. And watch out: עִיר (city) is feminine, even though its plural is עָרִים.
